pages.x: In the 1870s Argentina's ranches ended at a frontier in the pampas. Beyond it lived free Mapuche, Ranquel and Tehuelche peoples, who traded with the settlers and also raided their ranches for cattle and captives. In 1876 the war minister, Adolfo Alsina, began to dig a great ditch with forts across the plains to hold the line.

When Alsina died in 1877, the new war minister, General Julio Argentino Roca, said a ditch would never do. In 1879 some 6,000 soldiers marched south in five columns. Roca's own reached the Río Negro at Choele Choel on 25 May, Argentina's national day, and the river became the new frontier.
The army carried Remington rifles, which fired far faster than the old muzzle loaders, and strung telegraph wires behind it as it went.
pages.fx: Horsemen with lances and a few old guns could not stand against it, and wherever the columns went, the government in Buenos Aires knew within hours.

pages.x: From 1881 Colonel Conrado Villegas led columns up the rivers to Lake Nahuel Huapi and into the valleys of the Andes. At the same time Chile was conquering the Mapuche lands on its side of the mountains. Caught between two armies, the last free communities were hunted down one after another.

Thousands were killed in the campaigns. Many of the captured were shipped to the prison island of Martín García or sent to work on sugar plantations, men were put into the army, and women and children were handed out as servants to families in Buenos Aires, often never to see their own again.
pages.of: people captured and taken from their lands

pages.x: Valentín Sayhueque, lord of the apple country around Nahuel Huapi, held out longest. Starving and hunted, he surrendered with his people at Junín de los Andes on 1 January 1885. The war was over, and the lands of the south were sold off in vast estates.

The Tehuelche chief Inacayal, captured in 1884, was later taken with his family to the new museum of natural history in La Plata, where scientists studied them. He died there in 1888. His skeleton and brain were kept in the museum for over a century, until in 1994 his remains were returned to his people in Patagonia.

The campaign doubled the land Argentina really ruled and opened the south to sheep, cattle and European immigrants, and Roca was twice elected president. Today many Argentines see it as a conquest that took the land of Indigenous peoples and broke their families, and his statues have become a subject of argument.
